PC03-PREL1: Elian Morrow worked as an arbitration clerk for a company that made its living settling disputes before the workers involved could see the evidence. It was an earlier incarnation of Sabine Kade, well before the title and privileges that would later make her infamous. The body's ordinary pulse, unremarkable face and unmodified eyes passed unchallenged through offices where wealthier clients could not step without an entourage. In the first year, Elian learned that a signed consent form could be a weapon even when every letter on it was accurate. A report on a labour restitution fund vanished after a clinic operator manually corrected a beneficiary field in the personnel database. The database was not malfunctioning. Somebody was directing it to remember a different person. Elian copied the paper trail, paid a junior notary to witness the duplication and placed one version beyond company custody. The clerk's last day ended with a compulsory transfer that management described as a promotion and that nobody would discuss. Sabine can recall the smell of wet toner and the notary's expression, but cannot remember whether the notary survived.
PC04-PREL1: Mara Tress wore a cheap organic sleeve during the earliest district clearance campaigns. It was the first body in which Imani Voss learned to distinguish the order shouted over a radio from the people trapped under it. Mara coordinated volunteer evacuees, carried drinking water through chemical smoke and kept an account of who had entered each tunnel. When a commander ordered a sealed access hatch closed, the casualty spreadsheet already included a triage team as unrecoverable. Mara refused the order. The hatch stayed open long enough for a junior medic to walk out carrying another person's cortical stack. The official reprimand said the delay jeopardised the operation; the witnesses said it saved eleven people. Years later Imani would remember that the most important part was not defiance itself. It was a colleague choosing to remain beside her after the consequences were announced. A dispatch register, not a heroic legend, preserves the sequence. The body was eventually transferred under routine medical authority; its scars were lost, but its stubborn habit of counting the living followed the DHF.
PC04-PREL2: Kavi Serr was a port security medic who signed on for another sleeve because the previous body's exposure injuries had become impossible to repair. Kavi's hands knew how to strap a stretcher before the mind remembered learning it. The port was quieter than the evacuation zone, but its manifests were less honest. One sealed cargo vessel delivered a live cortical stack attached to a transfer order that claimed two different places of origin. The signature belonged to a technician Kavi had attended after a fatal accident, long before the document was supposedly issued. Another medic, frightened of losing a job with access to supplies, concealed the physical seal while Kavi copied the barcode. Neither dared accuse a named official, and neither knew the future significance of Project Palimpsest. When Kavi was moved to the next sleeve, the scan remained in an off-site emergency ledger. Imani's durable memory is of the younger medic asking whether a record can be true and a person still disappear from it. Kavi could not answer then. The question survives.
PC07-PREL1: Nalin Rao was an early neural-interface calibration inspector paid to reassure clients that updating a cortical stack's drivers changed no part of who they were. The inspection rig hummed in precise intervals; Nalin could recognise a defective connection by its rhythm alone. During an ordinary audit, three patients described childhood rooms identical in every object yet belonging to different families. One repeated a security phrase from a facility they had never entered. The employer called the coincidence a shared software artefact and ordered the logs purged as private medical data. Nalin retained the original checksum, the patient's refusal to consent to another scan, and the ticket number for the purge. The decision cost a promotion and made future assignments increasingly isolated. Even after a later transfer to a different body, Anik remembers the little red indicator that should have meant the recording was off. It remained lit long after the screen went dark. No testimony from this early case alone proves Palimpsest's later crimes, but it gives the investigators a verifiable method for distinguishing ordinary corruption from deliberate alteration.
PC08-PREL1: Ada Keene operated a pirate civic-radio channel from an unlicensed room behind a transit station. It was an early life in Solenne Pryce's chain, when the narrator had a voice but almost no audience. Families searched the district after violent sweeps with nothing more than ticket stubs and the names of people who had not come home. Ada read the names aloud, night after night, and archived every reply on magnetic tape because digital copies had a habit of vanishing. One carrier signal repeated a voice exactly like Ada's across two independently recorded transmissions, although the second broadcast originated somewhere she had never been. The voice gave a date that had not yet arrived. Ada stopped broadcasting for a month rather than frighten the families who trusted the station. A local courier later delivered a reel with a label in her own handwriting. Ada did not open it before the next sleeve transfer. Solenne remembers the weight of that unopened reel, not an answer to the mystery. The receipt for its transfer was witnessed by two people who could still be traced.
PC08-PREL2: Rene Vask wore an ordinary municipal-organic sleeve and took a desk job in complaints administration, hoping to discover where Ada Keene's missing persons had gone. The office treated bodies as allocations and cortical stacks as serial numbers. Rene learned the procedures well enough to know when they were being used to prevent a question from being asked. A mother arrived with a receipt proving her daughter's stack had been accepted into protected storage. The official reply described a newly issued sleeve, but never named the person inside it. When Rene asked which person had consented, the supervisor closed the case for lack of jurisdiction. The mother kept the only paper copy; Rene retained a carbon impression and the serial number. Both discovered later that the signing office had not existed on the recorded date. This older life's recurring feeling is not the satisfaction of solving a conspiracy but the dread of being told a completed form is an answer. It left Solenne with a stubborn preference for living witnesses over a perfect database entry.
